blocks.p: Then I saw in my dream that when Christian had reached the bottom of the hill, these good companions gave him a loaf of bread, a bottle of wine, and a cluster of raisins; and then he went on his way.

But now, in this Valley of Humiliation, poor Christian was hard pressed. He had gone only a little way when he saw a foul fiend coming across the field to meet him. His name is Apollyon. Christian began to be afraid, and to turn over in his mind whether to go back or to stand his ground. But then he considered that he had no armor for his back, and he thought that turning his back on the creature might give it all the more advantage to pierce him with its darts. So he decided to risk it and stand his ground. For, he thought, even if I had nothing more in view than saving my own life, the best thing would be to stand.

So he went on, and Apollyon met him. The monster was hideous to look at. He was covered with scales like a fish (they are his pride); he had wings like a dragon, feet like a bear, and out of his belly came fire and smoke, and his mouth was like the mouth of a lion. When he came up to Christian, he looked at him with contempt, and began to question him.
“Where have you come from? And where are you going?”
“I’ve come from the City of Destruction, which is the home of all evil, and I’m going to the City of Zion.”

“By this I see that you are one of my subjects, for all that country is mine, and I am its prince and its god. How is it, then, that you have run away from your king? If I didn’t hope you might still be of more use to me, I would strike you to the ground right now with a single blow.”

“I was born in your territory, it’s true,” said Christian, “but your service was hard, and your wages were more than a man could live on, ‘for the wages of sin is death.’ [Rom. 6:23] So when I came of age, I did what other thoughtful people do: I looked around to see if I could better myself.”

“No prince will lose his subjects so lightly,” said Apollyon, “and I will not lose you yet. But since you complain of your service and your wages, be content to go back, and whatever our country can offer, I promise here and now to give you.”
“But I have hired myself out to another, to the King of princes. How can I, in fairness, go back with you?”

“In this you have done what the proverb says: ‘traded a bad master for a worse.’ But it is common for those who have declared themselves his servants to give him the slip after a while and come back to me. Do the same, and all will be well.”
“I have given him my faith and sworn my allegiance to him. How can I go back on that and not be hanged as a traitor?”
“You did the same to me, and yet I am willing to overlook it all, if you will turn around now and go back.”

“What I promised you, I promised as a child. Besides, I believe the Prince under whose banner I now stand is able to release me from it, and to pardon what I did when I went along with you. And besides that, O destroying Apollyon, to tell you the truth, I like his service, his wages, his servants, his government, his company, and his country better than yours. So stop trying to persuade me. I am his servant, and I will follow him.”

“Think again, when your blood has cooled, about what you are likely to meet on the road you are taking. You know that most of his servants come to a bad end, because they are rebels against me and my ways. How many of them have been put to shameful deaths! And besides, you count his service better than mine, when he has never once come out of the place where he is to rescue any who served him from their enemies’ hands. But as for me, how many times, as the whole world well knows, have I rescued those who served me faithfully from him and his people, by force or by fraud, even after they had been captured? And so I will rescue you.”

“His holding back for now from rescuing them is on purpose, to test their love, whether they will cling to him to the end. And as for the bad end you say they come to, that is the most glorious thing of all in their eyes. They don’t much expect rescue in the present. They are waiting for their glory, and they will have it when their Prince comes in his own glory and the glory of the angels.”
“You have already been unfaithful in your service to him. How do you expect to be paid by him?”
“In what way, O Apollyon, have I been unfaithful to him?”

“You lost heart at the very start, when you were nearly choked in the Swamp of Despair. You tried wrong ways to get rid of your burden, when you should have waited until your Prince took it off. You fell into sinful sleep and lost your most precious possession. You were nearly persuaded to turn back at the sight of the lions. And when you talk about your journey, and about what you have heard and seen, deep down you are hungry for vain glory in everything you say and do.”

“All this is true,” said Christian, “and much more that you have left out. But the Prince whom I serve and honor is merciful and ready to forgive. Besides, I picked up these weaknesses in your country, for I drank them in there; and I have groaned under them, and been sorry for them, and have received my Prince’s pardon.”
Then Apollyon broke out into a terrible rage. “I am this Prince’s enemy! I hate him, his laws, and his people. I have come out for the very purpose of standing against you.”
“Apollyon, be careful what you do,” said Christian, “for I am on the King’s highway, the way of holiness. So watch yourself.”
Then Apollyon straddled the whole width of the road. “I have no fear in this matter. Prepare to die; for I swear by my den in hell that you will go no farther. Here I will spill your soul.”
And with that he threw a flaming dart at Christian’s chest; but Christian had a shield in his hand, and caught it, and so escaped that danger.

Then Christian drew his sword, for he saw it was time to act; and Apollyon came at him just as fast, throwing darts as thick as hail. In spite of all Christian could do to avoid them, Apollyon wounded him in the head, the hand, and the foot. This made Christian fall back a little. Apollyon pressed his attack with all his might, and Christian took courage again and resisted as bravely as he could. This fierce combat lasted for more than half a day, until Christian was nearly worn out; for you must understand that Christian, because of his wounds, could only grow weaker and weaker.
Then Apollyon, seeing his opportunity, began to close in on Christian, and wrestling with him, gave him a terrible fall; and with that, Christian’s sword flew out of his hand.

“I’m sure of you now,” said Apollyon. And with that he very nearly crushed him to death, so that Christian began to despair of his life. But, as God would have it, while Apollyon was drawing back for his last blow, to make a complete end of this good man, Christian quickly stretched out his hand for his sword and caught hold of it, saying, “Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will rise!” [Micah 7:8] And with that he gave him a deadly thrust, which made him fall back like one who has received his death wound. Christian, seeing this, came at him again, saying, “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” [Rom. 8:37] And with that Apollyon spread his dragon’s wings and sped away, and for a while Christian saw him no more. [James 4:7]

No one can imagine, unless he had seen and heard it as I did, what yelling and hideous roaring Apollyon made the whole time of the fight. He spoke like a dragon. And on the other side, what sighs and groans burst from Christian’s heart! I never once saw him give so much as a cheerful look the whole time, until he saw that he had wounded Apollyon with his two-edged sword. Then, indeed, he smiled and looked up. But it was the most dreadful sight I ever saw.

v: A match more unequal could hardly be:
a man must fight an angel. Yet you see
the valiant man, by wielding sword and shield,
makes him, though he’s a dragon, quit the field.

blocks.p: So when the battle was over, Christian said, “I will give thanks here to him who rescued me out of the mouth of the lion, to him who helped me against Apollyon.” And so he did, saying:

v: Great Beelzebub, the captain of this fiend,
designed my ruin, and toward that end
he sent him out in armor; and in rage
as hot as hell, he charged in to engage.
But blessed Michael helped me, and I,
by force of sword, soon made the monster fly.
So let me give to him unending praise,
and thank and bless his holy name always.

blocks.p: Then a hand came to him holding some of the leaves of the tree of life. Christian took them and laid them on the wounds he had received in the battle, and he was healed at once. He also sat down there to eat bread and to drink from the bottle that had been given him a little before. Then, refreshed, he set out on his journey again with his sword drawn in his hand; for he said, “For all I know, some other enemy may be close by.” But he met with no further attack from Apollyon all the way through this valley.

Now, at the end of this valley was another, called the Valley of the Shadow of Death, and Christian had to go through it, because the way to the Celestial City ran right through the middle of it. This valley is a very lonely place. The prophet Jeremiah describes it like this: “A wilderness, a land of deserts and pits, a land of drought and of the shadow of death, a land that no one” (except a Christian) “passes through, and where no one lives.” [Jer. 2:6]
Here Christian was harder pressed than in his fight with Apollyon, as you will see by what follows.
